name: Cyclofenil

lead: Cyclofenil is a nonsteroidal SERM that blocks estrogen signalling in the hypothalamus and pituitary, which increases LH and FSH release. It was introduced in France in 1970 as Ondogyne and used mainly to induce ovulation and treat menstrual disturbances.

In bodybuilding communities it was discussed alongside clomiphene and tamoxifen as a "post-cycle" option for restoring natural testosterone after steroid use, the idea being to hold on to muscle. A 2001 T Nation reply described it as similar to those drugs while knowing of no evidence it was better.

paras: Forum discussions from the early 2000s mention it as an alternative to clomiphene or tamoxifen in post-cycle routines, and older posters recall it being sold in powerlifting magazines in the 1980s. This page does not cover amounts, timing or sourcing.

Liver toxicity is the main concern: laboratory changes occur in a large share of users, and a minority develop hepatitis. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and liver disease. It is on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list and is marketed in only a few countries.

chain: Blocks estrogen feedback in the brain
Testes stimulated; aims to protect gains after steroid use
angle.text: Bodybuilders have discussed cyclofenil as a SERM for supporting natural testosterone after a cycle, so that muscle is kept. Published trials address other uses.

lead: Cyclofenil is a nonsteroidal selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) structurally related to clomifene and tamoxifen; it acts as a gonadotropin stimulant and ovulation inducer.[1] It was introduced for medical use in France in 1970 as Ondogyne and is now mostly discontinued, remaining available in Brazil, Italy and Japan.[1]

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding contexts it appears as a post-cycle therapy candidate: by blocking estrogen feedback at the brain, it raises LH and FSH, which stimulates the testes. The link to appearance runs through preserving muscle and recovering hormone levels after anabolic steroid use.[1][2]
Human trials of cyclofenil are mostly from gynecology and rheumatology, for ovulation, menopausal symptoms and scleroderma, not for muscle or physique.
infobox: Sexovid, Ondogyne, Fertodur, Neoclym and others
Prescription; marketed in a few countries

paras: Cyclofenil has been used for anovulatory infertility and menstrual disturbances from hypothalamic-pituitary insufficiency, and for menopausal symptoms.[1] Reviews describe it as a relatively weak SERM.[1]

T Nation posts from 2001-2008 list cyclofenil with clomiphene and tamoxifen as estrogen antagonists used with hCG to counter testosterone suppression.[3][4] One 2001 reply described it as similar to tamoxifen and clomiphene and said the author knew of no reason to prefer it or evidence it was as good.[5] Older posters recall a product sold under the name in the 1980s.[6]

The main concern is liver toxicity; biochemical liver changes occur in about 35 percent or more of users and about 1 percent develop overt hepatitis.[1] Contraindications include pregnancy, severe liver disease and unexplained uterine bleeding.[1] In a crossover trial in scleroderma, drop-outs included very high liver transaminases, and a case report describes haemolytic anaemia during treatment.[7][8]

Cyclofenil is a mixed agonist and antagonist at estrogen receptors, described as a relatively weak SERM that is generally less effective than other SERMs; it is considered an impeded estrogen.[1] By blocking estrogen action at the pituitary and hypothalamus it releases LH and FSH, which stimulates ovulation in women and can raise testosterone in men.[1]

Chemically it is a diphenylethylene derivative in which one phenyl ring is replaced by a cyclohexane ring, unlike the triphenylethylene SERMs clomifene and tamoxifen. It acts both centrally and peripherally, with an elimination half-life of 18 to 29 hours after a single dose.[1]

Wikipedia notes the drug is used by male athletes to raise testosterone, that it is not effective for that purpose in women, and that it is on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list; NFL lists also name it among anti-estrogenic agents.[1][9]

It has been sold in France, Germany, Mexico, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey and the UK in the past, under names including Sexovid, Ciclifen, Fertodur, Gyneuro, Klofenil, Menopax, Neoclym, Rehibin and others.[1]

A 1977 controlled trial compared cyclofenil, estradiol valerate and placebo in postmenopausal women.[10] Scleroderma research in the 1980s found it ineffective, a 1990 review listed it among therapies controlled studies had ruled out for generalised systemic sclerosis, and a Cochrane review examined it for Raynaud phenomenon.[1][7][11][12] No studies found of cyclofenil for muscle, physique or post-cycle recovery in men.
